cues.text: Let's turn to section six: the VitalNet lab and a CA NoSQL application.
Start with the problem.
Wearable devices generate telemetry in JSON, and that JSON is variable: different devices report different sensor attributes.
A document store suits this, because it can accommodate those differing attributes, while validation rules enforce the fields that must always be present.
For the lab, use synthetic data, never real patient records.
Each event should carry a unique event ID, which is used for deduplication.
It should also carry a timestamp, a pseudonymous patient identifier, a region, and the readings themselves.
One design rule matters here: design around your query patterns.
And avoid embedding an unbounded event array inside a single patient document, because that array would keep growing without limit.
Now the code sample, which is JavaScript in the MongoDB shell.
The first line creates an index on the telemetry collection, on the event ID field, in ascending order.
The option unique set to true means the database will reject a second document with the same event ID.
That is how deduplication is enforced.
The second statement inserts one document into the telemetry collection.
The event ID is "demo-001".
The patient ID is "P001".
The region is "Enugu".
The recorded-at field is a Date built from the ISO timestamp 2026, January the first, 09:00 UTC.
And the readings are a nested object, holding a heart rate of 82 and an SpO2 of 97.
SpO2 is blood oxygen saturation.
The last line is a query.
It finds documents where the patient ID is "P001", and sorts them by recorded-at with the value minus one, meaning descending, so the newest readings come first.
The source does not say this code was executed, so treat it as an illustration of the design, not as recorded output.
Next, some qualifications.
MongoDB uses BSON, not only JSON.
BSON is its binary storage format, which supports richer types than plain JSON.
A production design would validate ranges for the readings, use a suitable patient-and-time index, secure the cluster, and monitor ingestion.
Be careful about one tempting conclusion: a low CPU reading does not indicate correct design.
Instead, measure throughput, p95 latency, which is the latency that ninety-five percent of requests stay within, plus errors and storage growth.
And remember that SQL can also handle JSON and high-volume workloads.
NoSQL is a design option, not an automatic requirement.
Now the first essay question.
It reads: Design a cloud pipeline for real-time health telemetry.
Your answer should define the five Vs of big data.
It should explain Kafka ingestion, partitions and replay.
It should cover stream processing for alerts, document storage for recent operational data, and a governed lake and warehouse for historical analytics.
You must quantify volume, and discuss security, retention, idempotency, failover and cost.
Finally, conclude with explicit latency and consistency requirements.
The second essay question reads: Compare data lake, warehouse and federated database.
Define each one.
Compare them on schema, workload, governance and storage.
Demonstrate when raw heterogeneous data belongs in a lake, and when curated reports belong in a warehouse.
Finally, note that federated access preserves source autonomy, but can have network and performance limits.
Now the heading: Further platform and analytics revision.
Azure Cosmos DB illustrates a managed NoSQL platform with multiple APIs.
The API you select determines the data model and the query features you get.
Snowflake and BigQuery illustrate cloud analytics.
A data catalogue records datasets, schemas, owners and lineage, that is, where data came from and how it was transformed.
A metadata service supports discovery and governance.
Then two architecture styles.
Lambda architecture combines a batch layer and a speed layer.
Kappa-style designs instead emphasise stream processing and replay.
Both need deduplication, checkpointing and monitoring.
Finally, data quality.
Checks should validate completeness, correctness, freshness and uniqueness before analytics runs.
And in a health pipeline, failed events may be quarantined for review rather than silently dropped, so nothing disappears without someone being able to examine it.
